metadata.title: LOS DEBERES ESCOLARES. UN ANÁLISIS SISTEMATIZADO CON ESPECIAL REFERENCIA AL CASO ESPAÑOL

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a systematic analysis/review of the homework debate and does not report an original student-level large-scale assessment dataset extraction. It discusses international evidence using PISA and TIMSS as contextual references, but it does not describe an analytic sample, scaling, or plausible-value estimation procedure. Because no microdata analysis is conducted, there are no survey weights (e.g., student sampling/design weights) to apply or interpret for estimation. For any future empirical work using PISA/TIMSS microdata, analysts should apply the complex survey design weights provided in the international database and use the assessment’s official scaling/PV procedures for cognitive achievement outcomes.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not conduct an empirical predictive/achievement analysis on ILSA microdata; instead, it synthesizes prior research and secondary evidence (e.g., references to PISA/TIMSS and regional reports). Since there is no student-level dependent variable based on ILSA cognitive achievement scales, Plausible Values are not applicable to the study’s analysis. Missing-data handling is therefore not reported because no dataset is constructed for statistical estimation from ILSA microdata.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No original ILSA microdata sample is analyzed. The article synthesizes findings from prior meta-analyses and discusses Spain’s position using secondary references to PISA and TIMSS, alongside regional Spanish reports and other studies.

data.outcome_summary: This article is not an empirical machine-learning study; it is a systematic analysis of the homework debate with special reference to Spain. It synthesizes prior research (notably meta-analytic work by Cooper and others) and uses international large-scale assessment evidence (PISA and TIMSS) only as contextual background rather than as an analyzed microdata source. The paper reports qualitative/summary conclusions from the literature: homework shows a moderate correlation with school results in secondary education but little to no association in primary, and spending more than about two hours per day is described as counterproductive. It also emphasizes that homework is perceived as necessary by most students, teachers, and parents in Spain, and that homework types are linked to prevailing teaching styles and curricula. Methodologically, it does not provide ML model comparisons, performance metrics, or an explicit survey-weight/PV estimation pipeline because no original ILSA dataset is modeled.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse because the manuscript is a literature-based systematic analysis rather than an empirical study that trains or evaluates ML models on ILSA microdata. As a result, there is no analytic sample size, no country-level microdata counts, no plausible-value estimation, and no missing-data strategy to report. The paper’s contribution is conceptual/synthesizing (homework effects, perceptions, and policy/regulatory context), so ML technique fields and main findings for predictive targets are intentionally empty.
